Observable signals of fit are: willingness to check against batch, weight, and documents; asking follow-up questions when units conflict; keeping the original value and reason when revising records; and being able to hand a discrepancy to a supervisor for review in brief text. Signals requiring caution are: pursuing only speed and smoothing over differences by habit; calculating without checking units; ignoring site rules near equipment or goods; and filling in zeros on your own when a value is unknown. What is the difference between weighing records and sample registration?

Both are tasks this occupation may take on; the former focuses on readings and documents, the latter on numbers and sample destinations. The following is an editorial comparison and cannot replace equipment or sampling operating procedures.
Core purpose
Record material weight, quantity, and document discrepancies clearly so later receiving, shipping, or production records can be traced.
Match samples to the original batch and leave identification, storage, and transfer records.
Main objects and basis
Batch identification, scale or measuring tool readings, specifications, shipping documents, and declared weight; equipment suitability is confirmed on site.
Sampling instruction, batch, sample identification, container information, and designated recipient; do not design professional sampling plans on your own.
Core process
Check identity and unit, record the raw value, calculate by the rules, compare differences, and hand them to authorized personnel for confirmation.
Correspond the batch per instructions, register number and location, check labels, and record the transfer destination.
Main output
Raw readings, calculation results, discrepancy notes, and receiving and shipping records.
Sample registration forms, label check records, and handover records.
Responsible party
The operator is responsible for recording and reporting; equipment maintenance, quality determination, and goods disposal are divided according to actual authorization.
The operator keeps number correspondence and handover information; laboratory analysis and professional conclusions are borne by the relevant personnel.
How they work together
Check documents and discrepancies with receiving, shipping, and supervisors, and avoid losing records through verbal changes.
Check numbers and transfer conditions with the sampler, warehouse, and recipient, and report first when a mismatch is found.
Delivery boundary
Accurate records do not equal passed equipment verification or approved release.
Complete registration does not mean the sample is representative or passes testing; requests beyond your authority go to the supervisor for confirmation.
Key occupational judgments

These editorial self-check questions center on batch, unit, raw value, and anomaly responsibility. Answers must point back to the actual input; confirm unknown conditions first and do not invent data.
Do the physical goods, labels, and documents correspond to the same batch?
Are the reading unit, gross weight, and tare weight consistent?
Are the original value and reason retained after a retest or correction?
By which threshold and by whom should a discrepancy be confirmed?

First find the specification or instruction used for this task and confirm the threshold unit and the rule on including the equal sign; without a basis, list it as to be confirmed, and do not extend the exercise threshold to real goods.
Are sampling, lifting, or equipment operation within the authorized scope?

Check job training and site authorization; paper exercises do not authorize operating industrial equipment or handling hazardous materials. Requirements beyond scope go to the designated supervisor for confirmation.

Physical checking and recording may take place in warehouses, manufacturing sites, or weighing stations. The target job's equipment, shifts, lifting volume, and protection requirements should be checked separately; U.S. material cannot be used directly as a Chinese job condition.

Organization and location｜The work may connect warehouse offices with physical work areas. Weighing stations, receiving and shipping areas, and sample storage have different conditions, and the same job title may carry different site tasks.

Materials and tools｜Include scales, measuring tools, specification tables, labels, shipping documents, purchase orders, and electronic records. Check whether the tool suits the current object; training and equipment status are confirmed by site procedures, and software brands are not treated as uniform qualifications.
First identify the object and evidence for this time, then record, compare, and hand over; this is an editorial summary of the recording order, and actual procedures follow employer requirements.

Shifts and intensity｜U.S. material mentions repeated tasks, time pressure, and standing. A real job may also have night shifts, temperature, or lifting requirements, so ask about frequency and arrangements when applying. The paper experience covers only the recording part.
In anomaly communication, write the batch, reading, discrepancy, and pending items, and avoid saying only “the data is wrong”; keep the supervisor's reply and later corrections.

Review chain｜Raw values, calculations, retests, and reasons for change are kept separately. When labels and goods mismatch, report per procedure and do not change labels, release goods, or delete anomalies on your own. Handover records should state unresolved items.

Quality requirements｜The records of this occupation must point back to the goods, labels, and original documents. O*NET also lists tasks such as keeping the work area clean, exchanging information with customers or suppliers, forwarding sample orders, unloading and unpacking, and moving materials; not everyone does all tasks. For a real job, confirm site training, material conditions, and disposal authority, and do not treat a paper recording exercise as having completed this work.

subject.name: Weighers, Measurers, Checkers, and Samplers, Recordkeeping
subject.summary: Weighers, measurers, checkers, and samplers weigh, measure, and check materials, supplies, and equipment and keep records, and may also collect and register samples. This page uses the recordkeeping clerical scope of U.S. O*NET 43-5111.00, distinct from 51-9061, which focuses on production inspection. The core output is traceable quantity, weight, label, and anomaly records; Chinese jobs must be checked against actual duties.
